---
title: "Stage 1 — the study as data"
---

The protocol, expressed as JSON against a defined model, so that something other than a person
can read it.

## What this is

A USDM fragment is the part of the study definition the endpoints in scope actually need —
objectives, endpoints, estimands, arms, population, and the biomedical concepts the endpoints
are measured by. Not a whole digitised protocol, which is a separate and much larger job.

Loaded into the builder, the study looks like this:

![The study as the builder reads it. Note the rationale: this fragment was *generated* from the
M11-restructured protocol, and says by what and from which sections.](media/study-overview@739344c.jpg)

The fragment itself declares where it came from:

{{json:study/usdm/toriva-lung-301.usdm.json#study.versions[0].studyDesigns[0].arms[0]}}

That is one arm, exactly as stored. Every other element — objective, endpoint, estimand — has
the same character: a named thing with an identifier that something downstream can point at.

## What you do

1. Generate the fragment from the structured protocol, or hand-author it for a first pass.
2. Put it where the application looks for studies, and add it to the study manifest.
3. Open the application, and check the study card appears.
4. Open **Study Overview** and read each tab — Summary, Arms, Objectives & Endpoints, Schedule
   of Activities. These are your fragment, rendered.

## What you should see

A study card, and behind it the objectives and endpoints you put in, each with its text from the
protocol. If a tab is empty, that part of the fragment is missing or is not shaped the way the
reader expects.

## What to look out for

**Rendering is the real test, not schema validation.** A fragment can satisfy the schema and
still show an empty Arms tab, because the application reads a particular path and yours put the
content somewhere else that is equally valid. Load it and look before believing it.

**Hand-author once, then generate.** Writing a fragment by hand teaches the shape faster than
reading the model does, and it is worth doing once for that reason alone. But a hand-authored
fragment is a transcription of prose, and it inherits every ambiguity in the prose silently.
Generating it from a structured protocol makes the transcription step reviewable — and this
project's fragment went from one estimand to six when it was regenerated, because the structured
protocol carried what the prose had left to the analysis plan.
